name: Ordoliberalism
summary: Ordoliberalism holds that a competitive market is not self-sustaining but depends on a legal 'economic constitution' that the state must create and defend: it bans cartels and privileges, protects private property and contract, keeps money stable and policy rule-bound. The state shapes the rules of the game but does not steer economic processes, rejecting both laissez-faire and planning. It underlay West Germany's social market economy, with social security accepted as a complement to competition.
scope: The Freiburg School of Walter Eucken, Franz Böhm and Hans Großmann-Doerth and the postwar social market economy (Erhard), with Wilhelm Röpke's more conservative, Christian-communitarian strand. Statements on culture, religion, immigration and foreign policy are mostly outside the school and answered low-confidence; Röpke and the jurists differ on welfare and unions.

keyFigures.name: Walter Eucken
keyFigures.role: Founder of the Freiburg School and author of the principles of the competitive order

keyFigures.name: Franz Böhm
keyFigures.role: Jurist co-founder of the Freiburg School who developed the private law society and anti-privilege doctrine

keyFigures.name: Wilhelm Röpke
keyFigures.role: Economist associated with the school who called it liberal conservatism and shaped the social market economy debate

sources.title: Walter Eucken's principles of the competitive order
sources.author: Law & Liberty
sources.usedFor: Eucken constitutive and regulative principles: price system, property, free trade, stable money, liability, checks and balances, minimum wages and unions.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: A free, efficient price system is Eucken's fundamental principle and Röpke rejects planning in favour of price and competition, though both insist the market needs a legal framework.

public-ownership.rationale: Ordoliberals favoured privatising telecoms and similar firms and Röpke counts nationalization among socialism's failures, though natural monopolies may be supervised by the state.

unions-good.rationale: Eucken accepted unions within market limits, while Röpke repeatedly attacks union monopoly power over wages; adherents are split on whether they are simply good.

property-fundamental.rationale: Protection of private property is a constitutive principle for Eucken and Röpke calls property the pillar of the free order and warns against its erosion.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Cartels and concentrations of private power must be restrained by competition law, but the aim is a rule-based framework rather than general regulation of firms.

cut-welfare.rationale: Röpke argues the welfare state stifles responsibility and has outlived its need, while Eucken and the social market economy kept social security; adherents are split.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Not an ordoliberal topic; no basis in sources beyond general liberal presumptions versus Röpke's conservatism.

strong-leader.rationale: The 'strong state' means a state constrained by constitutional rules against interest-group capture, explicitly not an authoritarian one, and power must be checked.

state-harmful.rationale: The state is assigned the role of guardian of the competitive order and shaper of the economic constitution, so the school rejects anarchism.

decide-locally.rationale: Röpke champions decentralization and small communities as counterweights to concentration, and ordoliberals distrust concentrated state power.

traditional-family.rationale: Röpke treats the family and small communities as the base of a healthy society, but the Freiburg jurists said little about family, so the strands differ.

more-religion-public.rationale: Röpke deplores secularization and sees Christian tradition as the moral base of a free economy, but this is not shared across the Freiburg school.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Röpke values cultural inheritance and Western Christian civilization; the Freiburg jurists wrote little on national culture.

gradual-change.rationale: Röpke calls himself liberal-conservative and values stability, and Eucken stresses consistent policy, but the school is about constitutional design more than pace.

free-trade.rationale: Open markets and free trade are a constitutive principle, and Eucken noted that many cartels would vanish if tariffs went.

central-planning.rationale: Eucken and the Freiburg school rejected the centrally administered economy, citing Soviet socialism and Nazism as negative examples.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Böhm lists protective duties as privileges that violate the competitive order, and Eucken said tariffs foster cartels.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Ordnungspolitik rejects discretionary industrial policy: governments cannot pick winners and invite rent-seeking.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Röpke wants a broad class of independent small and medium owners and blames concentration for destroying it.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Money, prices and property are the basis of the competitive order and Röpke defends them.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: An independent central bank pursuing monetary stability is a core part of the model.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: The school opposes interest-group privileges and group-made rules; wages are left to employers and unions without state-set prices.

one-party-rule.rationale: Ordoliberals call for a constitutionally limited state with checks against arbitrary power and condemned Nazism.

democracy-best.rationale: Böhm pairs the private law society with a democratically structured constitutional state, though the school distrusts interest-group politics.

separate-church-state.rationale: Röpke wants Christian moral foundations while the school has no church-state doctrine.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Law is a general rule order for a private law society; scripture as source is not part of it.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The state is the guardian of the competitive order and its legal framework, so it must provide these functions.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Röpke blames class hatred and social religions, and the school rejects Marxist analysis.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Eucken allowed redistribution when outcomes become socially unacceptable but aims at a competitive order, not equal outcomes.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Rules channel self-interest toward good ends, but Röpke insists markets need a moral base beyond supply and demand.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Röpke stresses community while the Freiburg jurists stress individual rights under law; split.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Röpke criticizes mass society and concentration but welcomes the market economy's prosperity.

restore-past-order.rationale: Röpke is culturally conservative but the school is constitution-building, not restorationist.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Ordoliberals prefer binding rules to case-by-case discretion, but Vanberg justifies those rules by their good results, so rejection of judging by results is only partial.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Competitive prices and performance competition, not need, distribute goods.

production-for-use.rationale: Röpke defends profit and competition as justified instruments of the market order.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Röpke calls ownership, profit and competition justified and rejects socialism's technique.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Incompatible with a constitutional, privilege-free order and with Röpke's anti-collectivism.

collective-farming.rationale: Röpke favours dispersed independent owners and rejects collectivism.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Röpke argues collectivism, not the market, causes disorder, and values international economic cooperation.

taxation-theft.rationale: The school gives the state a legitimate role in funding the framework and accepts progressive taxation.

media-academia-power.rationale: The school did not make claims about universities or media holding political power, so neutral.

total-state.rationale: The school defined itself against Nazism and Soviet socialism and wants a state that shapes rules, not economic processes.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: The founders prized the break from feudal privilege to a private law society of equals.

bound-labor.rationale: Equal legal status and freedom of contract replace feudal bondage in their account.

single-common-good.rationale: Competitive order is treated as a public good yet interest groups are expected; split.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Röpke prefers independent property owners; co-determination is not part of the founders' program.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Keynesian demand management is a named negative example and rules over discretion in fiscal and monetary policy is central.

economic-freedom.rationale: Ordoliberals hold that economic power turns into political power, and Röpke says the market order underpins freedom and rule of law.

rule-by-example.rationale: The school wants government bound by general rules rather than relying on rulers' virtue.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Röpke defends religious and cultural foundations of civilization.

class-collaboration.rationale: Röpke condemns class hatred and the school gives employers and unions joint roles in wage setting.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Röpke defends inherited cultural institutions as part of the social fabric.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: A privilege-free order gives all persons the same legal status.

state-class-instrument.rationale: The state is meant to be guardian of the competitive order against privilege.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The school warns politicians yield to pressure groups, but does not call elites corrupt.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The founders distanced themselves from laissez-faire and gave the state an active role in shaping the economic constitution.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Equal legal status and freedom of contract oppose it.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Equal legal status for all persons and persons as ends in themselves are founding ideas.

socialism-one-country.rationale: A Marxist internal dispute; adherents reject socialism altogether.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Röpke values Christian foundations but the school has no education policy on religious instruction; split and undocumented.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Vanberg says citizens' consent is the measure of legitimacy of the economic constitution.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Performance competition is central, but struggle between peoples is not part of it.

separated-powers.rationale: Eucken's political order includes checks and balances against arbitrary power.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Eucken accepts social security and justice but not a priority claim.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Neither the Freiburg jurists nor Röpke in the opened text address ethnic diversity and cohesion directly.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: A free price system is fundamental and Erhard lifted price controls.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: The school wants rule-based European order but ordoliberals split on supranational union.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Röpke praises village and small-town life.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Liability for one's own choices is a constitutive principle, and the school favours no-bailout rules.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The school sees economic and political order as interdependent.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Politically independent central banks focused on price stability are a defining ordoliberal principle, reflected in Maastricht.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Wikipedia associates the school with progressive taxation.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Government by general rules and constitutional limits is the core of Ordnungspolitik.

common-currency.rationale: Ordoliberals favour rule-based monetary union but are split on the euro.

ban-cartels.rationale: Banning cartels and curbing private economic power is the defining task of the state as guardian of the competitive order.

no-bailouts.rationale: Liability for each actor's own choices is a constitutive principle and Vanberg cites bailouts as discretionary interventions to be denied.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Eucken rejected historicist and economic-determinist accounts, holding that the legal and political order shapes the economy and not the reverse.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Ordoliberalism rests on a constitutional framework binding even democratic majorities, with law and an independent judiciary protecting the competitive order.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Eucken's principles require open markets and free trade, and autarky and protectionism are rejected as privileges and distortions.

moral-incentives.rationale: The competitive price system, with private property and liability, is the coordinating mechanism; replacing material incentives is the opposite of the programme.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The school builds a lawful order through constitutional means and Roepke warns against collectivist upheaval, so revolution by arms is rejected.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Outside the school; ordoliberals wrote on economic order, and Röpke's conservative strand differs from the jurists.

patriotic-education.rationale: Outside the school; Röpke valued community and tradition while the Freiburg jurists focused on economic constitution, so views split.

public-money-creation.rationale: Ordoliberals want an independent central bank bound by rules for stable money, not discretionary state creation of money; commercial banking itself is accepted within that frame.

delink-world-market.rationale: Eucken's principles favor free trade and open markets as part of the competitive order.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Ordoliberals want an economic constitution that binds the state and is protected from political discretion, supporting entrenched guarantees such as property and contract.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Böhm's democratically structured constitutional state places lawmaking with an elected legislature under binding constitutional rules, which leans toward parliament over a monarch; the school never debated monarchy.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Röpke criticizes mass society and massification but not in terms of pacification to reproduce the social order; split.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Open markets and free trade are core principles of the competitive order, so extraction theories are rejected.

party-own-road.rationale: Indifferent to how socialist parties organize; the school opposes planning.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Eucken rejected centrally administered economies of every kind, covering both Nazi and Soviet types.

office-by-exam.rationale: The school addresses the economic order, not how public posts are filled; adherents are split.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Röpke's conservative strand favours stable marriage while the jurists were liberal; the school did not address it.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Ordoliberals accept social security as a complement to competition and differ on how to organise it.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Private property is one of Eucken's constituting principles of the competitive order, so communal land with use-based tenure is rejected.

single-official-language.rationale: The school did not address language policy; adherents are split.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Röpke's A Humane Economy criticises mass society and materialism as eroding the moral base of the free market.

corporate-influence.rationale: Ordoliberals saw interest-group and corporate capture of the state as a core threat to the competitive order, which is why they want an economic constitution that keeps privileges and cartels out of policy.

job-guarantee.rationale: Ordoliberals put monetary stability ahead of employment targets and reject state steering of the economy, so an employer-of-last-resort scheme runs against the framework.

industrial-unions.rationale: Ordoliberals worried about union monopoly power distorting the competitive order, so they would not favour industry-wide union structures; jurists and Röpke differ.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its value rests on accepting or rejecting common ownership of production, or on private property in general, and the statement now asks only whether personal belongings should stay private where production is held in common.

reviewHistory.rationale: Ordoliberals defend private property and contract and Röpke opposed nationalization, so common ownership of productive property is rejected.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its value rests on accepting or rejecting common ownership of production, or on private property in general, and the statement now asks only whether personal belongings should stay private where production is held in common.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

defeat-communism.rationale: Röpke was a forceful critic of collectivism and communism, and the school was formed against totalitarian planning.

religion-illusion.rationale: Röpke grounded the free economy in Christian and communitarian values, so a materialist account of religion is rejected.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Ordoliberalism calls itself a third way between laissez-faire and planning, but it takes the market economy as the sound basis, so it does not accept the statement as framed.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The economic constitution is a privilege-free, rule-bound order with equal legal status, which is incompatible with suppressing opposition.

alienated-labor.rationale: Röpke criticized proletarianization and mass society, but the school does not blame capitalism as such; adherents are mixed.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: The school favors rules that protect competition and equal legal status but also contractual freedom; no stated view.

social-market-economy.rationale: Ordoliberalism underlay West Germany's social market economy, combining competition rules with social security.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Ordoliberals insist on rule-bound, stable fiscal and monetary policy, so conditions that enforce discipline are broadly accepted.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Eucken's constituting principles call for constancy and predictability of rule-bound policy, and the school stresses rule of law.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: The Freiburg School held that concentrated private economic power undermines the competitive order and freedom, and wanted the state to break it up.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Ordoliberalism makes the strong state the guardian of law and order and the competitive framework.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Röpke stressed community and subsidiarity, but social security is accepted as a complement to competition, so adherents are split.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Outside the school; Röpke's Christian strand is conservative, the jurists silent, so split.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Outside the school; Röpke valued the traditional family but the Freiburg jurists did not address it, so split.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Ordoliberalism did not address local voting rights; Röpke's communitarian strand leans against while the liberal strand is indifferent, so it is split.

rent-control.rationale: Ordoliberals hold that prices must form freely in competition and reject price controls; Eucken's principles of the competitive order favor the price system, and rent caps distort it.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Foreign policy was outside the school; the postwar German social market economy accepted allied basing, but ordoliberals took no stated position.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Eucken accepted social security and competition rewards performance, but the school defends property income as part of the competitive order; the sources show it split.

culture-before-state.rationale: Röpke argued that moral and cultural foundations underpin the market, but the Freiburg jurists put the economic constitution first, so the school is split.

god-not-male.rationale: Ordoliberalism has no stated view on how God is described; adherents are split by personal belief.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Ordoliberalism requires a privilege-free competitive order open to all, so reserving economic life for a national majority contradicts equal competition and the ban on privileges.

independent-unions.rationale: The sources note the school split on unions, with concern about union market power balanced by freedom of association.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: Ordoliberals reject planning and state steering, but did not discuss what makes a society socialist.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Eucken allowed state regulation of natural monopolies, but the school mainly favours competition elsewhere; adherents split.

municipal-property.rationale: Private property and contract are protected pillars of the competitive order, and the school rejects collective ownership as well as planning.

person-over-state.rationale: Röpke's A Humane Economy and the school's concern for the dignity and freedom of the person treat the economy as serving people.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Röpke's Christian humanism holds that the market economy must be embedded in moral and spiritual foundations.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Eucken's liability principle holds that actors should bear the costs of their actions, and ordoliberals prefer market-conforming instruments to discretionary intervention.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Ordnungspolitik stresses transparent rules for the economy but the school never discussed treaty secrecy.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Eucken accepted redistribution within the competitive order, while Röpke opposed expansive welfare; the school is split.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Rule-bound policy and stable money are core principles of the competitive order, and the German debt brake draws on them.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Eucken's principles define one competitive order and reject mixing economic systems, so there is no open experimentation.

public-service-media.rationale: The school did not address public broadcasting; Röpke criticised mass culture while the German system emerged under the social market.

farm-price-support.rationale: The Freiburg School opposed privileges, subsidies and tariffs for particular groups, which counts against price guarantees; Röpke accepted some farm protection, so low confidence.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Eucken's liability principle makes polluters answer for harm, but ordoliberals also want the state to set framework rules rather than rely only on lawsuits, so the answer is mixed.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Ordoliberals favour state rules that internalise external costs, but Röpke also defended freedom and community; split.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: The school favours rules over discretion in the economic sphere, but did not address sentencing.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Eucken and Röpke reject central planning as incompatible with a competitive order and with freedom, so a planned state is not worth defending for its system.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: The school is about economic order; Röpke's conservative strand values rooted community, but the jurists do not, so adherents are split.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Ordoliberalism rests on a constitutional legal order with rule-bound state action, which excludes killing without trial.

self-ownership.rationale: Property and contract are protected in the economic constitution, but the school defends them as institutions of competitive order and limits them through competition law; split.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Social security is accepted as a complement to competition, and Röpke and the jurists differ on its design, so targeting versus universality is not settled.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Eucken and Böhm call for a privilege-free competitive order and bans on cartels, so special legal privileges for connected firms are the opposite of the programme.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Family law is outside the school; adherents differ.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: The Freiburg School built on marginalist economics and a competition-based price system, in which value comes from scarcity and demand, not labour.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Not a topic of the school; Roepke had a conservative patriotic strand but the jurists and economists took no stand.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Eucken's competitive order requires a rule-of-law state with no concentration of private or public economic power and rejects central administration of the economy, which excludes party-led socialism.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Röpke argues the welfare state stifles responsibility and has outlived its need, while Eucken and the social market economy kept social security; adherents are split. (Carried over from cut-welfare, "Welfare programs create dependency and should be cut.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: The state should prohibit cartels and break up concentrations of economic power in order to protect competition.
missingStatements.rationale: Banning cartels and curbing private economic power is the defining task of the state as guardian of the competitive order.

missingStatements.text: Governments should not grant special privileges, such as subsidies, tariffs or tax breaks, to particular firms or groups.
missingStatements.rationale: Böhm held that the state should on no account confer privileges, since this invites rent-seeking and undermines the privilege-free order.
missingStatements.declined: Covered by existing statements on tariffs-protect-industry and state-directs-investment, which ordoliberalism answers against.

missingStatements.text: Economic policy should follow fixed general rules rather than case-by-case discretion by officials.
missingStatements.rationale: Government by general rules instead of discretion is the core of Ordnungspolitik.
missingStatements.declined: Abstract rules-versus-discretion principle that nearly all ideologies would endorse in the abstract; too vague to separate ideologies.

missingStatements.text: Governments should not bail out failing banks or firms with public money.
missingStatements.rationale: Liability for each actor's own choices is a constitutive principle and Vanberg cites bailouts as discretionary interventions to be denied.

notes: Röpke and the Freiburg jurists diverge: Röpke is harsher on welfare and unions and culturally conservative, whereas Eucken accepted unions, minimum wages and redistribution within the competitive order. Source s1 is Wikipedia only for overview; the euro-crisis stance is not scored.
